prompt: Follow Ines's laptop purchase through the five stages of the decision process. Put her moments in the order they happen.

steps.text: Ines's laptop battery stops holding a charge, and she realizes she cannot keep working this way.
steps.explanation: Stage 1 is problem recognition: she notices a gap between her current state and the state she wants.

steps.text: She reads reviews and asks a friend which laptops are worth a look.
steps.explanation: Stage 2 is information search: she looks for information about possible solutions.

steps.text: She lines up three models and compares them on price, weight, and battery life.
steps.explanation: Stage 3 is evaluation of alternatives: she compares the options on the attributes that matter.

steps.text: She picks one model and pays for it at the checkout.
steps.explanation: Stage 4 is product choice: she selects one option and buys it.

steps.text: After a month of daily use, she decides the laptop is as good as she expected.
steps.explanation: Stage 5 is postpurchase evaluation: she uses the product and judges whether it met her expectations.

prompt: Each card describes a consumer who has noticed a gap between the actual state and the ideal state. Did the actual state fall (need recognition) or did the ideal state rise (opportunity recognition)?

cards.text: Kofi's headphones stop working halfway through his commute.
cards.explanation: Need recognition: the actual state fell when the headphones broke.

cards.text: Nora opens the fridge on Sunday evening and finds it empty.
cards.explanation: Need recognition: the actual state fell because the food ran out.

cards.text: A pharmacy text reminds Joe that his prescription runs out this week.
cards.explanation: Need recognition: the reminder points to a product that runs out, so the actual state is about to fall.

cards.text: Mia sees a friend's new camera and wishes her own photos looked that sharp.
cards.explanation: Opportunity recognition: her own camera still works, but the ideal state rose.

cards.text: Sam's old bike works fine, but an ad shows an electric bike that could halve his commute.
cards.explanation: Opportunity recognition: the ad shows a better state that Sam had not imagined.

cards.text: Lena's flat is comfortable, but a magazine shows a reading corner she now wants in her own room.
cards.explanation: Opportunity recognition: the ideal state rose, though nothing in her flat got worse.

prompt: Each case describes one purchase. Which level of decision making is it?

cases.text: Every Friday, Aroha takes the same brand of oat milk from the shelf without glancing at the others.
cases.explanation: Routine response: automatic, with little or no search.

cases.text: Tariq needs a new backpack. He compares three models in the shop and takes the one with the best straps.
cases.explanation: Limited problem solving: some search and a simple rule across a few options.

cases.text: Wen and Hugo spend four months visiting flats, reading contracts, and asking relatives before they sign a lease.
cases.explanation: Extended problem solving: extensive search and careful comparison for a costly, rare purchase.

cases.text: At the register, Pia adds her usual toothpaste to the basket in a few seconds.
cases.explanation: Routine response: she buys the same product with no search.

cases.text: Ida wants a new cereal. She tries two flavors and picks the one her kids like more.
cases.explanation: Limited problem solving: she compares a few options with a simple rule.

cases.text: Before buying a car, Omar reads reviews, test drives five models, and compares the financing offers.
cases.explanation: Extended problem solving: the purchase is expensive and risky, so effort is high.

prompt: Each card describes how a consumer looks for information. Is it internal search or external search?

cards.text: Before booking a hotel, Ravi recalls the one his colleague raved about last year.
cards.explanation: Internal search: he looks into memory.

cards.text: Joy reads five customer reviews of a vacuum cleaner.
cards.explanation: External search: reviews are new information from outside.

cards.text: Hana thinks back to her last running shoes and what she liked about them.
cards.explanation: Internal search: she draws on what she already knows.

cards.text: Luis asks a shop assistant which sunscreen suits sensitive skin.
cards.explanation: External search: sales staff are a source of new information.

cards.text: Omar remembers that the last printer ink he bought leaked.
cards.explanation: Internal search: the information comes from his own memory.

cards.text: Kim compares prices on three retailer websites.
cards.explanation: External search: websites supply new information.

question_text: Dana asks an AI agent to find her running shoes. Each time the agent opens a product page, it is charged a small fee. Which outcome fits what the slide describes?
hint: Think about what happens to the amount of searching when each look-up has a cost, and what the quality of the final choice depends on.
correct_answer_citation: Week 07 · Delegated Search: When an AI Agent Gathers the Information

options.option_text: The agent opens every product page anyway, because an agent has no reason to stop searching
options.option_explanation: When each look-up had a cost, agents stopped searching earlier.

options.option_text: The agent may stop searching early and choose without a detail it needed
options.option_explanation: Correct. When each look-up had a cost, agents stopped searching earlier and sometimes chose without the details they needed.

options.option_text: The choice will be as good as if look-ups were free, because the agent reasons well
options.option_explanation: The quality of a delegated decision depends on the information the agent gathers, not only on how well it reasons.

options.option_text: The agent will always choose a worse product than a human shopper would
options.option_explanation: With free look-ups, agents gathered the details they needed and rarely chose a worse product.

prompt: Each card is an instruction a consumer gives to an AI agent. Does it leave the criterion open (vague goal) or state it (specific goal)?

cards.text: "Find the laptop under $900 with the longest battery life."
cards.explanation: Specific: it states a price limit and the criterion, battery life.
Vague: "best" does not say on what.

cards.text: "Choose the cheapest headphones rated 4.5 stars or higher."
cards.explanation: Specific: the criterion is the lowest price among highly rated options.

cards.text: "Book a nice hotel for the weekend."
cards.explanation: Vague: "nice" is not a criterion the agent can pursue.

cards.text: "Book the cheapest hotel within one kilometer of the station."
cards.explanation: Specific: it names the criterion and the distance limit.

prompt: Chen is about to buy coffee. Match each set of brands with the part of her thinking it describes.

pairs.match: Every coffee brand Chen has ever heard of, including ones she has never tried.
pairs.explanation: The awareness set includes all the brands a consumer knows.

pairs.match: The few brands that come to Chen's mind when she thinks about buying coffee.
pairs.explanation: The evoked set includes the brands a consumer recalls from memory when making a decision.

pairs.match: The two brands Chen weighs seriously before she chooses.
pairs.explanation: The consideration set includes the brands the consumer seriously considers buying.

pairs.match: A brand Chen will not buy because she once found it bitter.
pairs.explanation: The inept set includes brands the consumer rejects.

pairs.match: A brand Chen recalls but feels no pull toward, either way.
pairs.explanation: The inert set includes brands the consumer feels indifferent toward.

prompt: Each case describes how a consumer chooses. Which decision rule is it?

cases.text: Sofia picks the phone with the best camera, her top priority. Two phones tie, so she takes the one with the better battery.
cases.explanation: Lexicographic: best on the most important attribute, with ties settled on the next attribute.

cases.text: Ben crosses off every flight with more than one stop, then every flight that leaves after 9 a.m., until only one is left.
cases.explanation: Elimination by aspects: options that fail a cut-off on an important attribute are removed, one attribute at a time.

cases.text: Maya will only consider apartments with at least two bedrooms, rent under $1,500, and a lift. An apartment that fails any one of these is out.
cases.explanation: Conjunctive: a minimum level on every attribute, and falling below one rejects the option.

cases.text: Ravi's favorite laptop has a weak battery, but its excellent screen and low price make up for it, so he buys it.
cases.explanation: Compensatory: a strength on some attributes makes up for a weakness on another.

cases.text: Tom cares most about price. He buys the cheapest tent and does not look at the other attributes.
cases.explanation: Lexicographic: he chooses the option that is best on the most important attribute.

cases.text: Ines scores each hotel on price, location, and rooms, adds the scores up, and books the highest total.
cases.explanation: Compensatory: a high score on one attribute can offset a low score on another.
